title: How to use this handbook
md:
Streaming feels hard because a few new ideas appear at once: data never ends, it arrives late and out of order, and the system must remember things between events. Once those ideas click, every streaming tool looks similar.

| Stage | Read | Goal |
|---|---|---|
| Foundations | Chapters 2–6 | Understand what streaming is, time, windows and watermarks |
| State and correctness | Chapters 7–9 | State, delivery guarantees, exactly-once, joins |
| Hands-on | Chapters 10–12 | Spark Structured Streaming end to end, with code |
| Wider view | Chapters 13–16 | Flink, Kafka Streams, cloud services, CDC |
| Design | Chapters 17–19 | Architectures, pipeline patterns, data quality |
| Production | Chapters 20– 24 | Monitoring, tuning, sizing, testing, troubleshooting |
| Revision | Chapters 25– 28 | Memory hooks, interview Q&A, coding questions, glossary |

> **The three ideas that unlock streaming:** (1) the data never ends, so you compute on **windows** of it; (2) events arrive **late and out of order**, so you decide how long to wait (**watermark**); (3) the system must **remember** things between events (**state**) and survive crashes without losing or double-counting (**checkpoints + idempotent sinks**).

title: What streaming is and when to use it
md:
#### Batch vs streaming in simple words

> **In simple words:** batch is like collecting all the day's letters and sorting them at night. Streaming is like a post office that sorts each letter the moment it arrives. Batch is simpler; streaming is faster.

|  | Batch | Streaming |
|---|---|---|
| Data | Bounded: a file, a day, a table | Unbounded: never ends |
| When it runs | On a schedule (hourly, daily) | Continuously, or in very frequent small batches |
| Latency | Minutes to hours | Milliseconds to minutes |
| Complexity | Lower | Higher: late data, state, ordering, 24×7 operations |
| Cost | Compute only while running | Usually always-on compute |
| Reprocessing | Rerun the job for a date | Replay from the source or from stored history |

#### Latency vocabulary

| Term | Typical latency | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Real-time (hard) | Microseconds–milliseconds | Engine control, trading systems (not data engineering) |
| Real-time / low latency | < 1 second | Fraud scoring, ad bidding |
| Near real-time | Seconds to a few minutes | Live dashboards, alerting, CDC replication |
| Micro-batch | Seconds to minutes per batch | Spark Structured Streaming default |
| Frequent batch | 15 min – 1 hour | Incremental batch jobs |

#### When streaming is worth it

- The **value of the data drops quickly**: fraud, outages, stock-outs, security threats, live operations.
- **Continuous sources** where batching only adds delay: clickstream, IoT, logs, CDC.
- **Event-driven products**: notifications, recommendations updated per action.

#### When it isn't

- Reports read once a day — an hourly or daily batch is simpler and cheaper.
- Heavy joins across many large historical tables — batch or incremental batch fits better.
- The team can't operate 24×7 systems yet.

> Ask the business **"what decision changes if the data is 1 minute old instead of 1 hour old?"** If nothing changes, you probably need incremental batch, not streaming.

#### The middle ground: incremental batch

Many "streaming" pipelines are really **incremental batch**: run every 15–60 minutes, process only new data, stop. Spark's `trigger(availableNow=True)` and Databricks Auto Loader make this easy: the same streaming code, run on a schedule, with checkpoints tracking what's done. It gives most of the freshness at a fraction of the operational cost.

title: Building blocks of a streaming system
md:
#### The pieces

```text
 PRODUCERS             TRANSPORT              PROCESSING             SINKS
 apps, devices,  ──►   Kafka, Event    ──►    Spark Structured  ──►  Delta / Iceberg,
 databases (CDC),      Hubs, Kinesis,         Streaming, Flink,      databases, caches,
 logs, APIs            Pub/Sub                Kafka Streams          Kafka, dashboards
                       (durable, partitioned, (state +               alerts
                        replayable)            checkpoints)
```

#### Events

An event is a fact about something that happened: "order 1001 placed at 10:00:01 for ₹2,500". Good events are:

- **Immutable** — you don't change past events; you add new ones.
- **Self-describing** — include an ID, an event timestamp, the entity key and a schema version.
- **Keyed** — the key (order ID, user ID, device ID) decides ordering and partitioning.

```text
{"event_id": "e-8f2c", "event_type": "order_placed", "event_ts": "2026-01-15T10:00:01Z",
 "order_id": 1001, "customer_id": 42, "amount": 2500.00, "schema_version": 3}
```

#### The log (transport)

A durable, partitioned, append-only log (Kafka and similar) sits between producers and processors:

- **Decouples** producers and consumers — they can fail, scale and deploy independently.
- **Buffers** spikes — if processing slows, events wait in the log instead of being lost.
- **Replays** — consumers can re-read history after a bug fix.
- **Orders** events per partition (by key).

#### Streams and tables (the duality)

> **In simple words:** a **stream** is the bank statement (every transaction); a **table** is the current balance. You can always compute the balance from the statement, and every change to the balance is a new line on the statement.

- Aggregating a stream by key gives a table (latest value / running total per key).
- The changes to a table form a stream (a changelog — exactly what CDC produces).

This duality explains CDC, log compaction, materialized views and stateful processing.

title: Time in streaming
md:
#### Three kinds of time

| Time | Meaning | Reliable for analytics? |
|---|---|---|
| **Event time** | When the event actually happened (inside the data) | Yes — the truth you usually want |
| Ingestion time | When the event entered the log/broker | Sometimes |
| **Processing** **time** | When the stream processor handles it | No — depends on delays, restarts, backlogs |

> **In simple words:** event time is when you **wrote** the letter; processing time is when the post office **sorted** it. If a letter sits in a mailbox for two days, sorting by arrival would put it on the wrong day.

#### Why events arrive late and out of order

- Mobile apps offline (flights, tunnels) send events hours later.
- Network retries and partitions.
- Gateways buffering IoT data during outages.
- Multiple sources with different delays.
- A stuck or restarted processor working through a backlog.

#### Event-time skew

The gap between event time and processing time is always moving: small in normal operation, huge after an outage. A correct streaming job must produce the same answer whether events arrive on time or after a 3-hour backlog — that is what event-time processing plus watermarks gives you.

> **Memory hook:** "Count by when it happened, not when it arrived."

title: Windows
md:
You can't "count all clicks" on a never-ending stream and finish. You count clicks **per window** — per 5 minutes, per hour, per user session.

> **In simple words:** a window is a bucket of time. Each event drops into the bucket(s) its timestamp belongs to; when a bucket is complete, you report its result.

#### Window types

```text
TUMBLING (fixed, no overlap)          |--10:00--|--10:05--|--10:10--|
  every event in exactly one window
SLIDING / HOPPING (fixed, overlapping) |----10:00-10:10----|
  size 10 min, slide 5 min                   |----10:05-10:15----|
  an event can be in several windows               |----10:10-10:20----|
SESSION (gap-based, per key)          [e e e e]  ...30 min gap...  [e e]
  window closes after inactivity       session 1                    session 2
GLOBAL (one window, custom trigger)    everything, emitted on a custom condition
```

| Window | Use for | Spark |
|---|---|---|
| Tumbling | Counts per minute/hour, periodic KPIs | `F.window("ts", "5 minutes")` |
| Sliding | Moving averages, "last 10 minutes, updated every minute" | `F.window("ts", "10 minutes", "1 minute")` |
| Session | User sessions, device activity bursts | `F.session_window("ts", "30 minutes")` |
| Global / custom | Count-based or rule-based triggers | Arbitrary stateful processing |

**Memory hook — "Tiles, Sliding doors, Sessions": tumbling** windows sit side by side like

> floor **tiles**; **sliding** windows overlap like **sliding doors**; **session** windows stretch like a phone call — they end when nobody talks for a while.

#### Window boundaries

- Windows are aligned to the epoch by default (10:00, 10:05…), not to the first event.
- A window `[10:00, 10:05)` includes 10:00:00 and excludes 10:05:00.
- Sliding windows multiply state and output: a 1-hour window sliding every minute keeps 60 windows per key.

title: Watermarks and late data
md:
#### The problem

If events can arrive late, when is a window "done"? Wait forever and you never produce results (and state grows without limit). Don't wait at all and late events are wrong or lost.

#### The watermark

> **In simple words:** a watermark is the "last entry" rule at a restaurant. "We'll accept guests up to 15 minutes late. After that, we close the bill." It's the system's estimate that **no more events older than this time will arrive**.

In Spark: **watermark = max event time seen so far − allowed lateness.**

```text
counts = (events
  .withWatermark("event_ts", "15 minutes")          # allowed lateness
  .groupBy(F.window("event_ts", "5 minutes"), "page")
  .count())
max event_ts seen = 10:32   allowed lateness = 15 min   → watermark = 10:17
window [10:10, 10:15) ends before 10:17 → finalized, emitted (append mode), state dropped
event at 10:12 arriving now            → older than watermark → dropped (too late)
event at 10:20 arriving now            → accepted, its window still open
```

#### What watermarks control

1. **When results are final** (append mode emits a window once the watermark passes its end).

2. **When state can be deleted** (keeps memory bounded).

3. **Which late events are dropped.**

#### Choosing the lateness

| Smaller watermark | Larger watermark |
|---|---|
| Lower latency for final results | More complete results |
| Less state, less memory | More state, more memory |
| More late events dropped | Results emitted later |

Measure it: compute the distribution of `processing_time − event_time` from real data and pick a lateness that covers, say, 99–99.9% of events.

#### Handling events later than the watermark

- **Accept the loss** for live dashboards (approximate is fine).
- **Batch correction**: land all raw events in a table, and recompute final numbers in a daily batch from the complete data — the "speed layer + correction" pattern.
- **Side output / late table**: some engines (Flink) route late events to a side output; in Spark, compare event time with a watermark yourself in `foreachBatch` and write late

events separately.

#### Multiple watermarks

When a query has several inputs (e.g. stream-stream join), Spark by default uses the **minimum** of the input watermarks (safe: waits for the slowest stream). It can be set to max (`spark.sql.streaming.multipleWatermarkPolicy=max`) to favour latency, at the risk of dropping data from the slower stream.

> **Memory hook:** "The watermark is the bouncer: late guests beyond the limit don't get in, and once the bouncer moves on, the old tables are cleared."

title: State and stateful processing
md:
#### Stateless vs stateful

| Stateless (each event alone) | Stateful (remembers across events) |
|---|---|
| filter, map, select, parse, enrich with a static table | aggregations, windows, deduplication, joins between streams, sessions, pattern detection |
| Easy to scale and recover | Needs a state store, checkpoints, cleanup (watermarks/timeouts) |

#### Where state lives

- **In memory with snapshots** (Spark's default HDFS-backed state store): fast, but state must fit in executor memory.
- **RocksDB** (embedded key-value store on local disk): handles much larger state with less GC pressure. Default choice for large state in Spark and Flink.
- State is checkpointed to durable storage so it survives failures.

```python norun
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass",
               "org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.RocksDBStateStoreProvider")
```

#### Keeping state bounded

State grows forever unless something removes it:

- **Watermarks** for windowed aggregations, dedup and joins.
- **Timeouts** for custom stateful logic (processing-time or event-time timeouts).
- **TTL** settings in newer APIs and in Flink.

> A stateful query without a watermark or timeout is a memory leak with a delay. Every stateful operator needs a rule for when state can be forgotten.

#### Arbitrary stateful processing

When built-in aggregations aren't enough (custom session logic, fraud velocity, alert cool-downs), write your own state logic per key:

- **PySpark:** `applyInPandasWithState` (Spark 3.4+); Spark 4.0 adds the more flexible `transformWithState` API with multiple state variables, timers and TTL.
- **Scala/Java:** `mapGroupsWithState` / `flatMapGroupsWithState`.
- **Flink:** `KeyedProcessFunction` with value/list/map state and timers.

```python norun
import pandas as pd
from pyspark.sql.streaming.state import GroupStateTimeout
def velocity(key, pdfs, state):
    count = state.get[0] if state.exists else 0
    for pdf in pdfs:
        count += len(pdf)
    state.update((count,))
    state.setTimeoutDuration(60 * 60 * 1000)          # forget a card after 1h of inactivity
    if state.hasTimedOut:
        state.remove(); return
    yield pd.DataFrame({"card_id": [key[0]], "txn_count": [count]})
out = (txns.groupBy("card_id")
       .applyInPandasWithState(velocity, outputStructType="card_id string, txn_count long",
                               stateStructType="count long", outputMode="update",
                               timeoutConf=GroupStateTimeout.ProcessingTimeTimeout))
```

> In real code, check `state.hasTimedOut` first — on a timeout call there are no new rows, and you remove the state and optionally emit a final result.

title: Delivery guarantees and exactly-once
md:
#### The three guarantees

| Guarantee | Meaning | Typical cause |
|---|---|---|
| At-most-once | Never duplicated, can be lost | Commit position before processing |
| **At-least-once** | Never lost, can be duplicated | Commit after processing; retries after failures — the common default |
| **Exactly-once** **(effectively-once)** | Each event affects the result once | Replayable source + checkpoints + idempotent/transactional sink |

> **In simple words:** at-least-once is a courier who might deliver the same parcel twice after a mix-up; exactly-once means the receiver checks the parcel ID and ignores the duplicate. "Exactly-once" is really **effectively-once**: duplicates may happen internally, but the final result counts each event once.

#### Where duplicates come from

1. **Producer retries** — a write succeeded, the ack was lost, the producer sends again.

2. **Consumer restarts** — processed but crashed before committing the position; reprocessed after restart.

3. **Upstream systems** — the source itself sends the same event twice (mobile SDK retries).

4. **Reprocessing / backfills** — replaying data into a sink that already has it.

#### The recipe: R·C·I

**Memory hook — R·C·I, "Really Careful Ingestion": R**eplayable source + **C**heckpointed

> progress + **I**dempotent (or transactional) sink. Miss any one and you get gaps or duplicates.

| Part | Spark / Kafka example |
|---|---|
| Replayable source | Kafka offsets, files in storage, Delta table versions |
| Checkpoint | Spark checkpoint: offsets + state + commit log per micro-batch |
| Idempotent sink | Delta (atomic commit per batch, batch IDs tracked), MERGE by key, upsert by primary key |

#### Idempotent sinks in practice

| Sink | How to make writes idempotent |
|---|---|
| Delta Lake | Built in for append (Spark records batch IDs); `foreachBatch` + MERGE by key for upserts; `txnAppId` + `txnVersion` options for idempotent writes inside `foreachBatch` |
| Relational database | Upsert by primary key (`MERGE`, `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT`); or store last batch ID per target |
| Key-value store / cache | `SET key = value` is naturally idempotent |
| Kafka (as sink) | Idempotent producer + transactions for Kafka-to-Kafka; otherwise consumers dedup by event ID |
| Files | Deterministic file names per batch; atomic rename/commit |
| External APIs | Idempotency keys (event ID) if the API supports them |

#### Deduplicating source duplicates

Even with exactly-once processing, if the **source** sends duplicates you must deduplicate on a business/event ID:

```text
deduped = (events.withWatermark("event_ts", "30 minutes")
                 .dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["event_id"]))      # Spark 3.5+
```

Or MERGE into the target by `event_id`, or use `ROW_NUMBER()` per key in silver.

title: Joins in streaming
md:
#### Stream–static join

```text
enriched = clicks.join(F.broadcast(dim_products), "product_id", "left")
```

- The static side is re-read each micro-batch (Delta tables pick up new versions), so dimension updates flow in.
- Cheap and common: enrichment with product, customer, device metadata.
- Inner and left outer (stream on the left) are supported.

#### Stream–stream join

Joins two unbounded streams — for example ad impressions with clicks, orders with payments.

```text
imp = impressions.withWatermark("imp_ts", "1 hour")
clk = clicks.withWatermark("click_ts", "2 hours")
joined = imp.join(clk, F.expr("""
    click_ad_id = imp_ad_id AND
    click_ts BETWEEN imp_ts AND imp_ts + INTERVAL 1 HOUR"""), "leftOuter")
```

- Both sides are buffered in state until a match is impossible.
- **Watermarks on both sides + a time-range condition** are required so state can be cleaned. Without them, state grows forever (and outer joins need them to emit unmatched rows).
- Left outer rows with no match are emitted only after the watermark passes — so they appear with a delay.

#### Joining with changing reference data

| Situation | Approach |
|---|---|
| Small dimension, changes occasionally | Stream–static join on a Delta table |
| Dimension changes often and history matters | Point-in-time lookup: SCD2 table joined on event time in `foreachBatch` |
| Very large dimension | Key-value lookup (cache/DB) inside `mapInPandas`/`foreachBatch`, batched |
| Dimension arrives as a stream (CDC) | Stream–stream join, or maintain it as a table (compacted topic / Delta) and use stream–static |

title: Spark Structured Streaming: the model
md:
> **In simple words:** Structured Streaming runs your normal DataFrame code again and again on small batches of new data, remembering where it stopped in a **checkpoint**. You write it almost like batch code.

#### The unbounded table

Each trigger, new rows are appended to an imaginary **input table**. Your query defines a **result table**. The **output mode** decides what is written to the sink each trigger.

```text
trigger 1: input rows 1–100   → result table v1 → write (append/update/complete)
trigger 2: input rows 101–180 → result table v2 → write changes
...        Spark computes only the incremental work, using state for aggregations
```

#### Micro-batch execution

1. Ask the source for new data since the last offsets (e.g. Kafka offsets, new files).

2. Write the planned offsets to the checkpoint's **offset log** (write-ahead).

3. Run the query on that batch as a normal Spark job (with state lookups/updates).

4. Write results to the sink.

5. Record the batch as done in the **commit log**.

If it crashes between 2 and 5, the restart re-runs the same batch with the same offsets — and idempotent sinks make that safe.

#### Triggers

| Trigger | Behaviour | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| Default (none) | Next batch starts as soon as the previous finishes | Lowest micro-batch latency |
| `processingTime="1 minute"` | One batch per interval | Steady, predictable load |
| `availableNow=True` | Process everything available now (in multiple batches), then stop | Scheduled incremental batch jobs |
| `once=True` | One batch then stop (older; prefer availableNow) | Legacy |
| `continuous="1 second"` | Experimental low-latency mode, limited operations (no aggregations) | Rarely used |

#### Output modes

| Mode | Writes | Works with |
|---|---|---|
| **append** | Only new final rows; aggregation rows only after the watermark passes the window | Stateless queries; windowed aggregations with watermark; stream-stream joins |
| **update** | Rows changed in this batch | Aggregations where the sink supports upserts (foreachBatch + MERGE) |
| **complete** The entire result table every batch |  | Small aggregations only (state never dropped) |

**Memory hook — "Add, Update, Copy everything": append** = only add finished rows;

> **update** = only changed rows; **complete** = rewrite the whole table every time.

#### Sources and sinks

| Sources | Sinks |
|---|---|
| Kafka / Event Hubs (Kafka API) / Kinesis (connector) | Delta / Parquet / files |
| Files in a directory (CSV, JSON, Parquet…); Auto Loader on Databricks | Kafka |
| Delta tables (as a stream of appends; change data feed for updates) | `foreachBatch` — any batch writer (JDBC, MERGE, multiple sinks) |
| Rate / rate-micro-batch (testing) | `foreach` (row-by-row, rarely needed) |
| Socket (testing only) | Console / memory (testing) |

title: Spark Structured Streaming: building pipelines
md:
#### A complete Kafka → bronze → silver → gold pipeline

```python norun
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window as W
# BRONZE: land raw events with Kafka metadata
raw = (spark.readStream.format("kafka")
       .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", BROKERS)
       .option("subscribe", "orders.events.v1")
       .option("startingOffsets", "earliest")          # used only when there's no checkpoint
       .option("maxOffsetsPerTrigger", 500_000)
       .load())
(raw.select(F.col("key").cast("string"), F.col("value").cast("string"),
            "topic", "partition", "offset", F.col("timestamp").alias("kafka_ts"))
    .withColumn("_ingest_ts", F.current_timestamp())
    .writeStream.format("delta")
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/orders_bronze")
    .trigger(processingTime="1 minute")
    .toTable("bronze.order_events"))
# SILVER: parse, validate, dedup
schema = "event_id STRING, order_id LONG, customer_id LONG, status STRING, amount
DECIMAL(18,2), event_ts TIMESTAMP"
parsed = (spark.readStream.table("bronze.order_events")
          .select(F.from_json("value", schema).alias("e"), "partition", "offset")
          .select("e.*", "partition", "offset"))
good = parsed.filter("event_id IS NOT NULL AND event_ts IS NOT NULL")
bad  = parsed.filter("event_id IS NULL OR event_ts IS NULL")
(bad.writeStream.format("delta").option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/orders_quarantine")
    .toTable("quarantine.order_events"))
(good.withWatermark("event_ts", "30 minutes")
     .dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["event_id"])
     .writeStream.format("delta").option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/orders_silver")
     .trigger(processingTime="1 minute").toTable("silver.order_events"))
# GOLD: 5-minute revenue per status (append after the watermark)
(spark.readStream.table("silver.order_events")
   .withWatermark("event_ts", "10 minutes")
   .groupBy(F.window("event_ts", "5 minutes"), "status")
   .agg(F.count("*").alias("orders"), F.sum("amount").alias("revenue"))
   .writeStream.format("delta").outputMode("append")
   .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/orders_gold_5m")
   .toTable("gold.orders_5m"))
```

#### Current state with foreachBatch + MERGE

```python norun
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
def upsert_orders(batch_df, batch_id):
    latest = (batch_df
      .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(
          W.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.desc("event_ts"), F.desc("offset"))))
      .filter("rn = 1").drop("rn"))
    (DeltaTable.forName(batch_df.sparkSession, "silver.orders_current").alias("t")
       .merge(latest.alias("s"), "t.order_id = s.order_id")
       .whenMatchedUpdateAll(condition="s.event_ts >= t.event_ts")   # ignore older events
       .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
       .execute())
(spark.readStream.table("silver.order_events")
   .writeStream.foreachBatch(upsert_orders)
   .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/orders_current")
   .trigger(processingTime="2 minutes").start())
```

Why this pattern matters:

- Deduplicate **within** the micro-batch (several events per key) before MERGE — MERGE fails if multiple source rows match one target row.
- The `event_ts >= t.event_ts` condition protects against out-of-order events overwriting newer state.
- If a batch is retried, the MERGE produces the same result — idempotent.

#### Writing one stream to several sinks

```python norun
def fan_out(df, batch_id):
    df.persist()
    df.write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("silver.events")
    (df.filter("severity = 'HIGH'")
       .select(F.col("event_id").alias("key"), F.to_json(F.struct("*")).alias("value"))
       .write.format("kafka").option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", BROKERS)
       .option("topic", "alerts.v1").save())
    df.unpersist()
stream.writeStream.foreachBatch(fan_out).option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/fanout").start()
```

> `foreachBatch` itself is at-least-once for external sinks — on a retry the same `batch_id` is processed again. Make each write idempotent, or record processed `batch_id`s in the target.

#### File sources and Auto Loader

```python norun
# open-source Spark file source
(spark.readStream.schema(schema).option("maxFilesPerTrigger", 500)
      .json("abfss://raw@lake.dfs.core.windows.net/events/"))
# Databricks Auto Loader: scalable discovery, schema inference and evolution
(spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles")
      .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
      .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", "/meta/schemas/events")
      .load("abfss://raw@lake.dfs.core.windows.net/events/"))
```

#### Reading a Delta table as a stream

```python norun
spark.readStream.table("silver.orders")                         # new appends only
spark.readStream.option("readChangeFeed", "true").option("startingVersion", 120) \
     .table("silver.orders")                                     # inserts, updates, deletes (CDF)
spark.readStream.option("skipChangeCommits", "true").table("t")  # ignore updates/deletes in source
```

A plain Delta stream fails if the source table has updates/deletes (they're not appends) — use change data feed or `skipChangeCommits` deliberately.

title: Spark Structured Streaming: operations
md:
#### Checkpoints

The checkpoint folder holds:

| Folder | Content |
|---|---|
| `offsets/` | Planned source offsets per batch (write-ahead log) |
| `commits/` | Batches that completed successfully |
| `state/` | State store files per operator and partition |
| `sources/` | Source-specific metadata (e.g. file source seen files) |
| `metadata` | Query ID |

Rules:

- **One checkpoint per query.** Never share, never copy between queries.
- Don't delete it to "fix" a problem — the query restarts from `startingOffsets` (reprocessing or skipping data).
- Store it on durable storage (cloud storage, HDFS), not local disk.
- Some code changes are **not compatible** with an existing checkpoint.

#### Which query changes are safe on restart?

| Change | Safe with the same checkpoint? |
|---|---|
| Filters, projections, adding columns to output (stateless) | Generally yes |
| Changing trigger interval, `maxOffsetsPerTrigger` | Yes |
| Adding/removing a Kafka topic to `subscribe` | Generally yes (new topic starts per `startingOffsets`) |
| Changing grouping keys, aggregations, window sizes, watermark column | **No** — state schema changes |
| Changing stream-stream join logic or dedup columns | **No** |
| Changing number of shuffle partitions for a stateful query | **No** — state is partitioned by it (it's fixed in the checkpoint) |
| Changing the sink type | Usually not |

For incompatible changes: start a **new checkpoint** and decide where to start — reprocess from bronze/earliest, or from a known offset/version — and make the sink idempotent so overlap is harmless.

#### Graceful stop and restart

```python norun
q = df.writeStream ... .start()
q.status          # is a batch running? waiting for data?
q.lastProgress    # input rows, rates, durations, offsets, state metrics
q.stop()          # stops after interrupting the current batch; safe with checkpoint + idempotent
sink
```

For a clean stop at a batch boundary, wait until `q.status["isTriggerActive"]` is false, then call `stop()`. In production, an external marker file or job control can request the stop.

#### Reading the progress metrics

```text
"numInputRows"            rows in this batch
"inputRowsPerSecond"      arrival rate
"processedRowsPerSecond"  processing rate         → must stay ≥ input rate over time
"durationMs.triggerExecution"   batch duration    → should be < trigger interval
"stateOperators[].numRowsTotal" / "memoryUsedBytes"  state size → must not grow forever
"sources[].startOffset / endOffset / latestOffset"   how far behind the source you are
```

#### StreamingQueryListener (monitoring hook)

```python norun
from pyspark.sql.streaming import StreamingQueryListener
class Monitor(StreamingQueryListener):
    def onQueryStarted(self, e): log.info("started %s", e.name)
    def onQueryProgress(self, e):
        p = e.progress
        push_metrics(p.name, p.inputRowsPerSecond, p.processedRowsPerSecond, p.batchDuration)
    def onQueryIdle(self, e): pass
    def onQueryTerminated(self, e):
        if e.exception: alert(f"stream {e.id} failed: {e.exception}")
spark.streams.addListener(Monitor())
```

#### Running streams in production

- Run each stream as its own job (or a few related queries per job) with **automatic restarts** (Databricks continuous jobs / retries, Kubernetes restart policy, YARN AM retries).
- Use **separate scheduler pools** or clusters for heavy streams so one doesn't starve another.
- Keep **bronze append-only** so any downstream stream can be rebuilt by replaying bronze.
- Compact small files regularly (OPTIMIZE, auto-compaction).

title: Other engines: Apache Flink
md:
#### What it is

Apache Flink is a distributed engine built for **true event-at-a-time streaming** (not micro-batch), with strong event-time and state support. It's widely used for low-latency, complex stateful applications.

#### Core concepts

| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| JobManager | Coordinates the job, checkpoints, recovery |
| TaskManager | Workers running parallel task slots |
| DataStream API | Low-level streaming API (Java/Scala; Python via PyFlink) |
| Table API / Flink SQL | Declarative SQL over streams and tables |
| Keyed state | Per-key value/list/map state, with TTL |
| Timers | Event-time or processing-time callbacks per key |
| Checkpoints | Periodic distributed snapshots (Chandy-Lamport style barriers) for exactly-once state |
| Savepoints | Manually triggered snapshots for upgrades, migrations, rescaling |
| Watermarks | Generated at sources with a strategy (e.g. bounded out-of-orderness) |
| Side outputs | Extra output streams, e.g. for late events |

#### Flink SQL example

```sql norun
CREATE TABLE clicks (
  user_id STRING, page STRING, ts TIMESTAMP(3),
  WATERMARK FOR ts AS ts - INTERVAL '10' SECOND
) WITH ('connector' = 'kafka', 'topic' = 'clicks', 'format' = 'json',
        'properties.bootstrap.servers' = 'broker:9092', 'scan.startup.mode' = 'latest-offset');
SELECT window_start, window_end, page, COUNT(*) AS views
FROM TABLE(TUMBLE(TABLE clicks, DESCRIPTOR(ts), INTERVAL '1' MINUTE))
GROUP BY window_start, window_end, page;
```

#### Spark Structured Streaming vs Flink

|  | Spark Structured Streaming | Apache Flink |
|---|---|---|
| Model | Micro-batch (continuous mode experimental) | Event-at-a-time |
| Typical latency | ~100 ms to minutes | Milliseconds to seconds |
| State & event time | Good; watermarks, RocksDB, arbitrary state APIs | Very rich: timers, TTL, side outputs, savepoints |
| Batch + streaming | Same DataFrame API, strong batch ecosystem | Unified too, but batch ecosystem smaller |
| Lakehouse integration | Excellent (Delta, Databricks) | Good (Iceberg, Paimon, Delta connector) |
| Python | First-class (PySpark) | PyFlink exists; Java/Scala most mature |
| Best for | Streaming ETL into the lakehouse, near- real-time analytics | Low-latency, complex event- driven apps, CEP |

> **Memory hook:** "Spark streams in buses (micro-batches leave every few seconds); Flink streams in taxis (each event goes immediately)."

title: Other engines: Kafka Streams, ksqlDB and cloud services
md:
#### Kafka Streams

A Java library (not a cluster) for Kafka-to-Kafka processing inside your application.

- **KStream** (event stream) and **KTable** (changelog/table), **GlobalKTable** (fully replicated lookup table).
- Local state stores (RocksDB) backed by changelog topics in Kafka — state is restored from Kafka after failures.
- Exactly-once with `processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2` (Kafka transactions).
- Scales by running more instances; parallelism limited by partitions.
- Great for microservices and Kafka-centric event processing; not for writing to a lakehouse.

#### ksqlDB

SQL over Kafka topics (streams and tables, persistent queries, materialized views) built on Kafka Streams. Good for simple filtering, joins and aggregations without writing Java.

#### Managed cloud services

| Cloud Transport | Processing |
|---|---|
| Azure Event Hubs (Kafka-compatible), IoT Hub | Azure Stream Analytics (SQL), Databricks, Fabric Real-Time Intelligence (Eventstream, KQL) |
| AWS Kinesis Data Streams, MSK (Kafka), Firehose (delivery) | Managed Service for Apache Flink, Glue streaming, EMR, Databricks |
| GCP Pub/Sub, Managed Kafka | Dataflow (Apache Beam), Dataproc, Databricks |

#### Apache Beam / Dataflow

Beam is a programming model (Java/Python/Go) with one API for batch and streaming, run on runners like Google Dataflow or Flink. It popularized the key streaming questions: **what** is computed, **where** in event time (windows), **when** in processing time results are emitted (triggers), and **how** refinements relate (accumulation).

**Memory hook — Beam's four questions: "What, Where, When, How": What** results

> (transforms), **Where** in event time (windows), **When** to emit (watermarks + triggers), **How** to refine (accumulate or discard).

title: Streaming transport: Kafka-style logs in brief
md:
(Detailed in the Kafka handbook; the essentials for any streaming design.)

| Concept | Why it matters for streaming |
|---|---|
| Topic partitions | Unit of parallelism and ordering |
| Key → partition | Same key, same partition → per-key order |
| Offsets | Consumer position; the basis for replay and exactly-once |
| Consumer groups | Parallel consumption; max parallelism = partitions |
| Retention | How far back you can replay; must exceed worst-case downtime |
| Compaction | Keeps latest value per key — current-state topics, CDC |
| Schema Registry | Enforces compatible schema evolution between producers and consumers |
| DLQ topics | Park bad records without blocking the partition |

#### Partitioning decisions

- Key by the entity whose events must stay ordered (order_id, user_id, device_id).
- Avoid hot keys (one giant customer, a default "unknown" key) — they create one overloaded partition and one slow task.
- Plan the partition count for peak throughput and future growth; changing it later breaks key → partition mapping.

#### Kinesis and Pub/Sub differences

|  | Kafka | Kinesis Data Streams | Pub/Sub |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unit of parallelism | Partition | Shard | Managed (no partitions to manage) |
| Ordering | Per partition | Per shard | Per ordering key (opt-in) |
| Replay | By offset/time within retention | By sequence number/time within retention | Seek to timestamp/snapshot (with retention enabled) |
| Delivery to consumer | Pull | Pull (or enhanced fan- out push) | Push or pull, ack-based |

title: Change Data Capture (CDC)
md:
#### What CDC is

> **In simple words:** CDC is a stream of "what changed" in a database — every insert, update and delete — read from the database's transaction log, in commit order.

#### CDC approaches

| Approach | How | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Log-based** (Debezium, native CDC, cloud DMS) | Read the transaction log (binlog, WAL, redo, SQL Server CDC) | Captures every change incl. deletes; low source load; ordered | Setup and permissions; log retention to manage |
| Query-based (timestamp polling) | `WHERE updated_at > last_watermark` | Simple | Misses deletes and intermediate changes; needs reliable timestamps; source load |
| Trigger-based | DB triggers write to audit tables | Captures everything | Adds load and complexity to the source |
| Snapshot diff | Compare full snapshots | Works anywhere | Expensive, coarse, slow |

#### A CDC event

```text
{"op": "u",
 "before": {"id": 42, "city": "Bangalore", "tier": "silver"},
 "after":  {"id": 42, "city": "Bengaluru", "tier": "gold"},
 "ts_ms": 1768471200123,
 "source": {"db": "crm", "table": "customers", "lsn": "0000a1f2:00012ab3:0004"}}
```

`op`: `c` create, `u` update, `d` delete, `r` snapshot read.

#### Applying CDC correctly

1. **Order by the source position** (LSN / binlog position / SCN), not by arrival time.

2. **Deduplicate per key per batch** — keep only the latest change per key for current-state tables.

3. **Guard against old changes** — only apply if the incoming position is newer than the stored one.

4. **Handle deletes** — hard delete in current-state tables; close the version in SCD2 history.

5. **Keep the raw changelog** in bronze for audit and rebuilds.

```python norun
def apply_cdc(batch, batch_id):
    latest = (batch.withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(
                 W.partitionBy("id").orderBy(F.desc("lsn")))).filter("rn = 1"))
    (DeltaTable.forName(batch.sparkSession, "silver.customers").alias("t")
       .merge(latest.alias("s"), "t.id = s.id")
       .whenMatchedDelete(condition="s.op = 'd' AND s.lsn > t.lsn")
       .whenMatchedUpdateAll(condition="s.op <> 'd' AND s.lsn > t.lsn")
       .whenNotMatchedInsertAll(condition="s.op <> 'd'")
       .execute())
```

On Databricks, declarative pipelines offer `AUTO CDC` / `APPLY CHANGES` with `SEQUENCE BY` and `STORED AS SCD TYPE 1/2`, which implements these rules for you.

#### Initial snapshot + streaming changes

CDC tools first take a **consistent snapshot** of existing rows, then stream changes from the log position at snapshot time. Downstream must treat snapshot rows (`op = r`) as inserts/upserts and then apply the stream — with ordering by position preventing the snapshot from overwriting newer changes.

#### Outbox pattern

Services write business changes and an "outbox" event row in the **same DB transaction**; CDC publishes outbox rows to Kafka. This avoids the dual-write problem (DB updated but event not sent, or vice versa).

title: Streaming architectures
md:
#### Lambda architecture

```text
             ┌─► batch layer: full recompute nightly (accurate) ─────┐
Sources ─► log                                                        ├─► serving (merge views)
             └─► speed layer: streaming (fast, approximate) ─────────┘
```

- Pros: accurate final results, fast recent results.
- Cons: **two code paths** for the same logic, hard to keep consistent.

#### Kappa architecture

```text
Sources ─► log (long retention) ─► ONE streaming path ─► serving tables
                 └─ reprocess = replay the log with new code into a new table, then switch
```

- Pros: one code base.
- Cons: replay of long history can be slow and needs long retention (or a lakehouse copy).

#### Streaming lakehouse (most common today)

```text
Kafka / Event Hubs / CDC ─► BRONZE Delta (raw, append, replayable forever)
                         ─► SILVER Delta (parsed, deduplicated, MERGE/CDC applied)
                         ─► GOLD Delta (aggregates, facts, features)
                                      │
             dashboards · ML · APIs · reverse-ETL · alerts
Same code runs continuously, or as availableNow incremental batches.
Reprocessing = replay from bronze, not from the broker.
```

> **Memory hook:** "Lambda has two kitchens (fast and slow) cooking the same dish; Kappa has one kitchen that can re-cook from the recipe log; the lakehouse keeps every ingredient in the pantry (bronze) so it can always re-cook."

#### Choosing latency per layer

Not everything needs to be real time. A common design: bronze and silver streaming (minutes), gold aggregates as frequent batch, daily corrections from the complete data.

title: Common streaming pipeline patterns
md:
| Pattern | What it does | Key techniques |
|---|---|---|
| Ingest to lake | Land events from Kafka/files to bronze | Append, checkpoints, keep offsets/metadata |
| Clean & conform | Parse, validate, dedup, standardize | Explicit schemas, quarantine/DLQ, dedup with watermark |
| Real-time aggregation | KPIs per window | Tumbling/sliding windows, watermark, append mode |
| Sessionization | Group events into sessions | Session windows or custom state with timeouts |
| Enrichment | Add reference data | Stream–static joins, broadcast, periodic refresh |
| CDC replication | Keep a current-state table in sync | Order by LSN, MERGE, deletes, SCD2 history |
| Alerting / anomaly | Detect conditions and notify | Windows, thresholds, rate-of-change, cool-down state |
| Velocity features | Counts/sums per key over recent time | Stateful per-key processing with timeouts |
| Stream-stream correlation | Match related events (impression → click) | Watermarks on both sides, time-bound join |
| Fan-out | One stream to many sinks | `foreachBatch`, idempotent writes per sink |
| Late-data correction | Make final numbers complete | Live approximate + batch recompute from silver |
| Dead letters | Keep bad events without blocking | DLQ topic / quarantine table + alerts + replay tool |

#### Alert with cool-down (sketch)

```python norun
def raise_alerts(batch, batch_id):
    candidates = batch.filter("avg_value > threshold")
    recent = spark.table("gold.alerts").filter("alert_ts > current_timestamp() - INTERVAL 30
MINUTES")
    new = candidates.join(recent.select("device_id", "rule"), ["device_id", "rule"], "left_anti")
    new.withColumn("alert_ts",
F.current_timestamp()).write.mode("append").saveAsTable("gold.alerts")
```

title: Data quality in streaming
md:
#### Where checks run

| Stage | Checks |
|---|---|
| Producer / schema registry | Schema compatibility, required fields |
| Bronze → silver | Parse success, required fields not null, valid types/ranges, duplicates |
| Silver → gold | Business rules, referential checks against dimensions |
| Continuous monitors | Volume per minute vs baseline, freshness (event-time lag), null rates, DLQ rate |

#### Handling bad records

- **Never block a partition on one bad event** — route it to a DLQ/quarantine with the error reason, and continue.
- Count quarantined records per batch and alert when the rate exceeds a threshold.
- Keep a replay path: fix the bug, then reprocess quarantined events.

#### Freshness and completeness metrics

- **Event-time lag:** `now − max(event_ts)` in the target — how stale the data is.
- **Source lag:** latest source offset − processed offset.
- **Volume:** events per minute vs the same minute last week; sudden drops often mean a producer bug.

title: Monitoring and alerting
md:
#### The golden signals for a stream

| Signal | Healthy | Alert when |
|---|---|---|
| Source lag (records / time) | Stable, small | Growing for N minutes |
| Input vs processing rate | Processing ≥ input on average | Processing consistently below input |
| Batch duration vs trigger | Duration < trigger interval | Duration > trigger for several batches |
| State size | Stable (bounded) | Growing without limit |
| Event-time freshness | Within SLA | Data older than SLA |
| Query status | Active | Terminated / restarting repeatedly |
| DLQ / quarantine rate | Near zero | Spike |
| Output volume | Within baseline | Sudden drop or spike |

#### Tools

- Spark: `lastProgress`, `StreamingQueryListener`, Spark UI "Structured Streaming" tab, Databricks streaming metrics.
- Kafka: consumer lag exporters; managed-service consoles (Event Hubs, MSK, Confluent).
- Dashboards in Grafana / Datadog / Azure Monitor; alerts to PagerDuty/Teams/Slack.

> Monitor **lag in time**, not only in records — "10 minutes behind" means something to the business; "2 million records behind" doesn't.

title: Performance tuning
md:
#### Throughput

- Enough **source partitions** (Kafka partitions) for parallelism at peak.
- `minPartitions` (Kafka source) to split large Kafka partitions into more Spark tasks.
- Right-size **shuffle partitions** for stateful queries — fixed in the checkpoint, so choose before first run (e.g. 2–3× total cores).
- **Rate limits**: `maxOffsetsPerTrigger` / `maxFilesPerTrigger` / `maxBytesPerTrigger` to keep batch sizes stable and recover gracefully from backlogs.
- Avoid Python UDFs in hot paths; use built-in functions or pandas UDFs.

#### Latency

- Shorter triggers (or default trigger) and smaller batches.
- Fewer stateful operators and shuffles; broadcast small dimensions.
- RocksDB state store for large state (less GC); **changelog checkpointing** in newer RocksDB providers reduces checkpoint time.
- Avoid writing huge numbers of small files each batch — balance trigger interval with file size.

#### State

- Always bound state (watermark/timeout).
- Store aggregates, not raw lists of events.
- Watch `numRowsTotal` and memory per state operator.

#### Sinks

- Delta: optimized writes / auto-compaction; scheduled OPTIMIZE; liquid clustering on query keys.
- MERGE in `foreachBatch`: keep target clustered on the merge key; include partition/date predicates in the condition to limit files scanned.
- Databases: batch writes, upserts, connection pooling; don't write row by row.

#### Backlog recovery

After an outage, a stream may face hours of backlog. With rate limits it catches up steadily instead of attempting one giant batch. Scale up temporarily (autoscaling or more workers), then scale back.

title: Sizing a streaming pipeline
md:
#### Start from throughput

```text
peak_rate (MB/s)  = events_per_second_at_peak × avg_event_size
kafka_partitions  ≈ peak_rate / per_partition_throughput × headroom (1.5–2)
                    (per-partition throughput ≈ 5–10 MB/s — measure it)
cores             ≈ peak_events_per_sec / events_per_sec_per_core (measured in a test)
```

#### Worked example

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Average rate | 20,000 events/s; peak 3× = 60,000 events/s |
| Event size | 1 KB → peak ~60 MB/s |
| Kafka partitions | 60 MB/s ÷ ~5 MB/s ≈ 12 → with headroom **24–48** |
| Processing per core (parse + dedup + window, measured) | ~5,000 events/s |
| Cores at peak | 60,000 ÷ 5,000 = 12 → with headroom **~20–24** **cores** |
| Cluster | 3–4 workers of 8 cores (autoscale 2–5) |
| State | ~5M active keys × ~200 bytes ≈ 1 GB (+ overhead) → RocksDB, comfortable |
| Shuffle partitions (stateful) | ~2–3× cores → **48–64**, fixed in checkpoint |

#### Volume per day → average rate

| Daily volume | Average | Typical peak (≈3×) |
|---|---|---|
| 10 GB | ~0.12 MB/s | ~0.35 MB/s |
| 100 GB | ~1.2 MB/s | ~3.5 MB/s |
| 1 TB | ~11.6 MB/s | ~35 MB/s |
| 5 TB | ~58 MB/s | ~175 MB/s |

> Always validate with a load test at peak rate plus a **backlog test** (stop the stream for an hour, restart, and measure how long it takes to catch up).

title: Testing streaming pipelines
md:
#### Unit test the transformation as batch

Write transformations as functions on DataFrames; test them with batch DataFrames — the same function works on a stream.

```python norun
def clean_events(df):
    return (df.filter("event_id IS NOT NULL")
              .withColumn("amount", F.col("amount").cast("decimal(18,2)")))
def test_clean_events(spark):
    df = spark.createDataFrame([("e1", "10.5"), (None, "3")], "event_id string, amount string")
    assert clean_events(df).count() == 1
```

#### Test streaming behaviour

- **Memory source / rate source** and `trigger(availableNow=True)` to run a stream to completion in tests.
- Write input files in steps, run the stream, assert output after each step — test late data, duplicates, and restarts with the same checkpoint.
- Test **restart idempotency**: run, kill midway, restart with the same checkpoint, check no duplicates or gaps.

```python norun
q = (spark.readStream.schema(schema).json(input_dir)
       .transform(clean_events)
       .writeStream.format("delta").option("checkpointLocation", chk)
       .trigger(availableNow=True).start(out_dir))
q.awaitTermination()
assert spark.read.format("delta").load(out_dir).count() == expected
```

title: Troubleshooting
md:
| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Lag keeps growing | Processing slower than input; skewed partition; slow sink | Scale cores/partitions, fix hot keys, speed up sink, remove UDFs |
| Batch duration > trigger interval | Too much data per batch, heavy MERGE, state too big | Rate limits, optimize MERGE (clustering, predicates), RocksDB |
| State grows forever | Missing watermark/timeout; watermark column not in grouping | Add watermark/timeout; include event-time window/column correctly |
| Aggregates never appear in append mode | No watermark, or watermark not advancing (no new data) | Add watermark; understand that results emit only after the watermark passes |
| Duplicates in target | At-least-once retries, source duplicates, non-idempotent foreachBatch | Dedup on event ID, MERGE by key, idempotent writes |
| Data missing after restart | Checkpoint deleted/changed; retention expired; `failOnDataLoss=false` hid it | Keep checkpoints stable, longer retention, bronze copy for replay |
| Query fails after a code change | Incompatible change with the checkpoint (state schema) | New checkpoint + controlled reprocessing |
| Many tiny files | Short triggers, many partitions | Longer triggers, optimized writes, compaction |
| MERGE error: multiple source rows matched | Several events per key in one batch | Keep latest per key in the batch before MERGE |
| Stream-stream join uses huge memory | Missing watermarks or time-range condition | Add both, and tighten the time bound |
| Out-of-order updates overwrite newer data | Applying by arrival, not by event/sequence | Condition MERGE on newer event time / LSN |

title: Remember it: memory hooks for streaming
md:
#### The story: the 24-hour post office

1. **The letter box (producer → log).** Letters (events) are dropped into numbered slots by postcode (partition by key). The slots keep letters for 7 days (retention), and anyone can re-read them (replay).

2. **The date stamp vs the sorting time.** Each letter has the date it was written (event time). The sorter notes when it was sorted (processing time). Reports always go by the written date.

3. **Sorting trays (windows).** Letters go into trays by hour written (tumbling), into overlapping trays for "last 3 hours" (sliding), or into a tray per person that closes when they stop writing for a while (session).

4. **The closing bell (watermark).** "We accept letters up to 1 day late." Once the bell rings for a day, that day's tray is sealed and reported; later letters are set aside.

5. **The ledger (state).** For each customer, the clerk keeps a running total. Old pages are torn out when nobody needs them (state cleanup).

6. **The logbook (checkpoint).** "Last letter processed: slot 7, number 4,512." After a power cut, work resumes from #4,513.

7. **The receipt check (idempotent sink).** Every parcel has an ID; the receiver ignores IDs already received. That's how duplicates don't double-count (exactly-once).

8. **The returns shelf (DLQ).** Unreadable letters go to a shelf with a note, so the line keeps moving.

#### One-look anchors

| Concept | Picture | Hook |
|---|---|---|
| Stream vs table | Bank statement vs balance | Statement → balance; balance changes → statement |
| Event time | Date written on the letter | Count by when it happened |
| Tumbling window | Floor tiles | Side by side, no overlap |
| Sliding window | Sliding doors | Overlapping views |
| Session window | Phone call | Ends after silence |
| Watermark | Closing bell / bouncer | How late is too late |
| State | The clerk's ledger | Remember, then forget on time |
| Checkpoint | The logbook | Resume exactly where you stopped |
| Exactly-once | Receipt check | R·C·I |
| DLQ | Returns shelf | Park bad events, keep moving |
| Micro-batch vs event-at- a-time | Bus vs taxi | Spark vs Flink |

#### Mnemonics

| Mnemonic | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **R·C·I** — Really Careful Ingestion | Replayable source + Checkpoint + Idempotent sink = exactly- once |
| Tiles, Sliding doors, Sessions | Tumbling, sliding, session windows |
| Add, Update, Copy everything | Append, update, complete output modes |
| What, Where, When, How | Beam's four questions: results, event-time windows, triggers, refinements |
| Count by when it happened, not when it arrived | Use event time |
| Every state needs a way to forget | Watermarks, timeouts, TTL |
| Lag in minutes, not in messages | Monitor time lag for the business |
| **L·O·D·S** of late data | **L**imit with watermark, **O**utput late to a side table, **D**aily batch correction, **S**ize lateness from real delay data |

title: Interview questions and answers
md:
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Batch vs streaming? | Bounded vs unbounded data; scheduled vs continuous; minutes– hours vs seconds latency; streaming adds state, late data and 24×7 operations |
| Event time vs processing time? | When it happened vs when it's processed; use event time for correct analytics |
| What is a watermark? | Max event time seen minus allowed lateness; decides when windows are final, when state is dropped, and which late events are discarded |
| Tumbling vs sliding vs session windows? | Fixed non-overlapping; fixed overlapping; gap-based per key |
| How do you handle late data? | Watermark sized from measured delays; late events to a side table; batch recompute for final numbers |
| Exactly-once in Spark? | Replayable source + checkpointed offsets/state + idempotent sink (Delta / MERGE); dedup source duplicates on event ID |
| Append vs update vs complete? | Only final new rows; changed rows; whole result each time |
| What's in a checkpoint? | Offsets (WAL), commits, state, source metadata |
| Which code changes break a checkpoint? | Changes to stateful logic: grouping keys, aggregations, windows, joins, dedup keys, shuffle partitions |
| Stream–static vs stream– stream joins? | Static side re-read each batch, cheap; stream–stream buffers both sides and needs watermarks + time bounds |
| What is foreachBatch for? | Running batch writers per micro-batch: MERGE upserts, JDBC, multiple sinks — must be idempotent |
| How do you size Kafka partitions? | Peak throughput ÷ per-partition throughput, plus headroom; also ≥ desired consumer parallelism |
| Spark vs Flink? | Micro-batch vs event-at-a-time; Spark for lakehouse ETL and near real time; Flink for low latency and complex state |
| Lambda vs Kappa? | Two paths (batch + speed) vs one streaming path with replay; lakehouse with bronze replay is today's common middle ground |
| How do you apply CDC correctly? | Order by source LSN, latest per key per batch, apply only newer positions, handle deletes, keep raw changelog |
| How do you monitor a stream? | Lag (time), input vs processing rate, batch duration, state size, freshness, DLQ rate, query status |
| Stream is falling behind — what do you check? | Spark UI for skew/slow stages, sink duration, batch size, UDFs, partitions; then scale, rate-limit, fix hot keys |
| availableNow vs continuous streaming? | availableNow processes the backlog then stops — scheduled incremental batch with streaming guarantees, cheaper than 24×7 |

#### Scenario questions

| Scenario | Strong answer |
|---|---|
| "Dashboard counts jump after a stream restart." | Duplicates from reprocessed batches — make the sink idempotent (Delta append / MERGE by event ID), dedup source duplicates with a watermark |
| "We changed the window size and the stream won't start." | Stateful change incompatible with the checkpoint — new checkpoint, reprocess from bronze for the needed period, idempotent sink |
| "Mobile events arrive up to 2 days late." | Live windows with a short watermark for the dashboard; all events land in silver; daily batch recompute for final metrics |
| "State memory keeps growing in production." | Missing or ineffective watermark/timeout; check the grouping includes the event-time window; switch to RocksDB; store aggregates not raw events |
| "Business wants real time but reads the report once a day." | Propose incremental batch (availableNow every 15–60 min) — same freshness for their use, lower cost and complexity |
| "One Kafka partition is far behind the others." | Hot key or skew — check key distribution, change key or add salt, increase partitions, or split work with `minPartitions` |

title: Streaming coding questions with answers
md:
These are the hands-on questions asked in data engineering coding rounds and take-home tasks. Each has the question, a working answer in PySpark Structured Streaming (one in plain Python), and the points the interviewer is checking. Try each one yourself before reading the answer.

All answers assume:

```python norun
from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window as W
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
BROKERS = "broker1:9092,broker2:9092"
```

#### Q1. Read a Kafka topic, parse JSON and land it in Delta

Topic `orders.v1` has JSON values: `order_id, customer_id, amount, status, event_ts`. Land parsed records in `bronze.orders`, restartable without losing or duplicating data.

```python norun
schema = "order_id LONG, customer_id LONG, amount DECIMAL(18,2), status STRING, event_ts
TIMESTAMP"
orders = (spark.readStream.format("kafka")
          .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", BROKERS)
          .option("subscribe", "orders.v1")
          .option("startingOffsets", "earliest")
          .load()
          .select(F.from_json(F.col("value").cast("string"), schema).alias("o"),
                  "partition", "offset", F.col("timestamp").alias("kafka_ts"))
          .select("o.*", "partition", "offset", "kafka_ts"))
q = (orders.writeStream.format("delta")
     .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/bronze_orders")
     .outputMode("append")
     .trigger(processingTime="1 minute")
     .toTable("bronze.orders"))
```

**Checking:** `value` is binary → cast to string; explicit schema; a unique checkpoint; `startingOffsets` only applies on first start; keeping partition/offset for traceability.

#### Q2. Events per page in 5-minute windows

From `silver.clicks (page, user_id, event_ts)`, count events per page in 5-minute tumbling windows. Events can be up to 10 minutes late. Write final results only.

```python norun
counts = (spark.readStream.table("silver.clicks")
          .withWatermark("event_ts", "10 minutes")
          .groupBy(F.window("event_ts", "5 minutes"), "page")
          .count()
          .select(F.col("window.start").alias("window_start"),
                  F.col("window.end").alias("window_end"), "page", "count"))
(counts.writeStream.format("delta").outputMode("append")
   .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/page_counts_5m")
   .toTable("gold.page_counts_5m"))
```

**Checking:** watermark **before** the aggregation on the same event-time column; append mode emits a window only after the watermark passes its end; flattening the `window` struct.

#### Q3. Moving average with a sliding window

Per device, compute the average temperature over the last 10 minutes, updated every minute.

```text
avg_temp = (readings
  .withWatermark("reading_ts", "5 minutes")
  .groupBy("device_id", F.window("reading_ts", "10 minutes", "1 minute"))
  .agg(F.avg("temperature").alias("avg_temp_10m"), F.count("*").alias("readings")))
```

**Checking:** window(duration, slide) syntax; each reading belongs to 10 windows, so state and output are 10× a tumbling window — mention the cost.

#### Q4. Remove duplicate events

The mobile SDK retries, so the same `event_id` can arrive several times within 30 minutes. Deduplicate without unbounded state.

```text
deduped = (events
  .withWatermark("event_ts", "30 minutes")
  .dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark(["event_id"]))          # Spark 3.5+
# Before Spark 3.5: include the event-time column so state can be cleaned
deduped_old = (events.withWatermark("event_ts", "30 minutes")
                     .dropDuplicates(["event_id", "event_ts"]))
```

**Checking:** plain `dropDuplicates(["event_id"])` without a watermark keeps every ID forever (memory leak). With the older API, duplicates must share the same `event_ts` to be removed.

#### Q5. User sessions with a 30-minute inactivity gap

Group each user's clicks into sessions that end after 30 minutes of inactivity. Output session start, end, number of events.

```text
sessions = (clicks
  .withWatermark("event_ts", "10 minutes")
  .groupBy("user_id", F.session_window("event_ts", "30 minutes"))
  .agg(F.count("*").alias("events"),
       F.min("event_ts").alias("session_start"),
       F.max("event_ts").alias("last_event")))
(sessions.writeStream.format("delta").outputMode("append")
   .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/sessions").toTable("silver.sessions"))
```

**Checking:** `session_window` (Spark 3.2+); a session is emitted only after the watermark passes its end (last event + gap) — sessions appear with a delay. For complex session rules, use arbitrary stateful processing.

#### Q6. Enrich a stream with a dimension table

Add product name and category to each click from `silver.products` (Delta, updated daily).

```python norun
products = spark.read.table("silver.products").select("product_id", "product_name", "category")
enriched = (spark.readStream.table("silver.clicks")
            .join(F.broadcast(products), "product_id", "left"))
```

**Checking:** stream–static join; the Delta table is re-read every micro-batch, so daily updates flow in; broadcast avoids a shuffle; left join keeps clicks with unknown products.

#### Q7. Join impressions with clicks

Match each ad impression with a click on the same ad within 1 hour. Keep impressions with no click (for CTR).

```text
imp = (impressions.select("imp_id", F.col("ad_id").alias("imp_ad_id"), "imp_ts")
                  .withWatermark("imp_ts", "2 hours"))
clk = (clicks.select("click_id", F.col("ad_id").alias("click_ad_id"), "click_ts")
             .withWatermark("click_ts", "3 hours"))
joined = imp.join(clk, F.expr("""
            click_ad_id = imp_ad_id AND
            click_ts >= imp_ts AND
            click_ts <= imp_ts + INTERVAL 1 HOUR"""), "leftOuter")
```

**Checking:** watermarks on **both** streams plus a **time-range** condition — otherwise state grows forever and outer rows are never emitted. Unmatched impressions appear only after the watermark passes the 1-hour limit.

#### Q8. Keep only the latest status per order (upsert)

`silver.order_events` streams status changes. Maintain `gold.orders_current` with one row per order and its latest status. Events can arrive out of order.

```python norun
def upsert(batch_df, batch_id):
    latest = (batch_df
      .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(
          W.partitionBy("order_id").orderBy(F.desc("event_ts"))))
      .filter("rn = 1").drop("rn"))
    (DeltaTable.forName(batch_df.sparkSession, "gold.orders_current").alias("t")
       .merge(latest.alias("s"), "t.order_id = s.order_id")
       .whenMatchedUpdateAll(condition="s.event_ts > t.event_ts")
       .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
       .execute())
(spark.readStream.table("silver.order_events")
   .writeStream.foreachBatch(upsert)
   .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/orders_current")
   .trigger(processingTime="1 minute").start())
```

**Checking:** window functions aren't allowed on a streaming DataFrame directly, but inside `foreachBatch` the batch is a normal DataFrame; dedup within the batch before MERGE; the timestamp condition stops older events overwriting newer state; idempotent on retries.

#### Q9. Apply CDC events from a database

A topic carries Debezium-style events `{op, before, after, lsn}` for `customers`. Keep `silver.customers` in sync, including deletes.

```python norun
cdc_schema = """op STRING, lsn STRING,
                before STRUCT<id: LONG, name: STRING, city: STRING>,
                after  STRUCT<id: LONG, name: STRING, city: STRING>"""
def apply_cdc(batch_df, batch_id):
    ev = (batch_df.select(F.from_json(F.col("value").cast("string"),
cdc_schema).alias("e")).select("e.*")
          .withColumn("id", F.coalesce("after.id", "before.id")))
    latest = (ev.withColumn("rn",
F.row_number().over(W.partitionBy("id").orderBy(F.desc("lsn"))))
                .filter("rn = 1")
                .select("id", "op", "lsn", "after.name", "after.city"))
    (DeltaTable.forName(batch_df.sparkSession, "silver.customers").alias("t")
       .merge(latest.alias("s"), "t.id = s.id")
       .whenMatchedDelete(condition="s.op = 'd' AND s.lsn > t.lsn")
       .whenMatchedUpdate(condition="s.op <> 'd' AND s.lsn > t.lsn",
                          set={"name": "s.name", "city": "s.city", "lsn": "s.lsn"})
       .whenNotMatchedInsert(condition="s.op <> 'd'",
                             values={"id": "s.id", "name": "s.name", "city": "s.city", "lsn": "s.lsn"})
       .execute())
(spark.readStream.format("kafka").option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", BROKERS)
   .option("subscribe", "crm.customers").load()
   .writeStream.foreachBatch(apply_cdc)
   .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/customers_cdc").start())
```

**Checking:** order by source position (LSN), not arrival; latest per key per batch; only apply newer LSNs (replays are harmless); deletes take the key from `before`. Note: LSNs must be in a sortable, fixed-width format.

#### Q10. Top 3 pages per 5-minute window

Find the top 3 pages by views in each 5-minute window, continuously.

```python norun
# Sorting/limit/ranking aren't supported on streaming aggregates in append mode.
# Aggregate in the stream, rank inside foreachBatch.
views = (clicks.withWatermark("event_ts", "10 minutes")
               .groupBy(F.window("event_ts", "5 minutes"), "page").count())
def top3(batch_df, batch_id):
    w = W.partitionBy("window").orderBy(F.desc("count"))
    (batch_df.withColumn("rnk", F.row_number().over(w)).filter("rnk <= 3")
       .write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("gold.top_pages_5m"))
(views.writeStream.outputMode("append").foreachBatch(top3)
   .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/top_pages").start())
```

**Checking:** knowing what streaming doesn't support (`orderBy`, `limit`, window functions on streams) and the `foreachBatch` workaround. With append mode, each window reaches `foreachBatch` once, when final.

#### Q11. Distinct users per window

Count distinct users per 1-minute window.

```text
# countDistinct is not supported on streaming DataFrames
uniq = (clicks.withWatermark("event_ts", "5 minutes")
              .groupBy(F.window("event_ts", "1 minute"))
              .agg(F.approx_count_distinct("user_id").alias("approx_users")))
# exact alternative (Spark 3.4+): one row per (window, user), then count rows per window
per_user = (clicks.withWatermark("event_ts", "5 minutes")
                  .groupBy(F.window("event_ts", "1 minute").alias("w"), "user_id").count())
exact = (per_user.groupBy(F.window(F.window_time("w"), "1 minute").alias("w"))
                 .agg(F.count("*").alias("users")))
```

**Checking:** `countDistinct` isn't supported in streaming; approximate (HyperLogLog) is usual; the exact version chains two time-window aggregations using `window_time` (Spark 3.4+) — correct, but keeps much more state. (A plain `dropDuplicates(["w", "user_id"])` would never clean its state, because the watermark column isn't in the keys.)

#### Q12. Alert when a device is too hot

Raise an alert when a device's temperature is above 80 °C in at least 3 readings within 10 minutes. Don't alert the same device more than once per 30 minutes.

```python norun
hot = (readings.filter("temperature > 80")
       .withWatermark("reading_ts", "5 minutes")
       .groupBy("device_id", F.window("reading_ts", "10 minutes"))
       .agg(F.count("*").alias("hot_readings"))
       .filter("hot_readings >= 3"))
def raise_alerts(batch_df, batch_id):
    recent = (spark.table("gold.device_alerts")
              .filter("alert_ts > current_timestamp() - INTERVAL 30 MINUTES")
              .select("device_id"))
    new = (batch_df.select("device_id", "window", "hot_readings")
                   .dropDuplicates(["device_id"])
                   .join(recent, "device_id", "left_anti")
                   .withColumn("alert_ts", F.current_timestamp())
                   .withColumn("batch_id", F.lit(batch_id)))
    new.write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("gold.device_alerts")
(hot.writeStream.outputMode("append").foreachBatch(raise_alerts)
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/device_alerts").start())
```

**Checking:** filtering before aggregating (less state); windowed count; cool-down using a `left_anti` join against recent alerts; storing `batch_id` to detect retries.

#### Q13. Send bad records to a quarantine table

Some Kafka messages aren't valid JSON or miss required fields. Keep good records flowing and park bad ones.

```text
parsed = (raw.select(F.col("value").cast("string").alias("raw"), "partition", "offset")
             .withColumn("o", F.from_json("raw", schema)))
good = (parsed.filter("o IS NOT NULL AND o.order_id IS NOT NULL AND o.event_ts IS NOT
NULL")
              .select("o.*", "partition", "offset"))
bad  = (parsed.filter("o IS NULL OR o.order_id IS NULL OR o.event_ts IS NULL")
              .select("raw", "partition", "offset", F.current_timestamp().alias("quarantined_at")))
good.writeStream.format("delta").option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/good").toTable("silver.orders")
bad.writeStream.format("delta").option("checkpointLocation",
"/chk/bad").toTable("quarantine.orders")
```

**Checking:** `from_json` returns null (or a struct of nulls) for bad input — it doesn't fail; never block the stream on bad data; separate checkpoints per query; keep the raw value for replay after a fix.

#### Q14. Run a stream as a scheduled incremental job

New JSON files land in a folder all day. Process them every hour, then stop the job to save cost.

```python norun
(spark.readStream.schema(schema)
      .option("maxFilesPerTrigger", 1000)
      .json("abfss://raw@lake.dfs.core.windows.net/orders/")
 .writeStream.format("delta")
      .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/orders_hourly")
      .trigger(availableNow=True)
      .toTable("bronze.orders")
 .awaitTermination())
```

**Checking:** `availableNow` processes everything new, possibly in several batches, then stops; the checkpoint remembers which files were processed; scheduled by Airflow/ADF/Databricks Jobs. On Databricks, Auto Loader (`format("cloudFiles")`) scales file discovery better.

#### Q15. Stream changes (including updates and deletes) from a Delta table

`silver.orders` gets MERGE updates. Stream every change to a downstream table.

```python norun
spark.sql("ALTER TABLE silver.orders SET TBLPROPERTIES (delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true)")
changes = (spark.readStream.format("delta")
           .option("readChangeFeed", "true")
           .option("startingVersion", 120)
           .table("silver.orders")
           .filter("_change_type IN ('insert', 'update_postimage', 'delete')"))
```

**Checking:** a plain Delta stream only handles appends and fails on updates/deletes; change data feed gives `_change_type`, `_commit_version`, `_commit_timestamp`; skip `update_preimage` unless you need old values.

#### Q16. Running total per customer that survives retries

Maintain total spend per customer from a payments stream. Retries must not double-count.

```python norun
def add_totals(batch_df, batch_id):
    sums = batch_df.groupBy("customer_id").agg(F.sum("amount").alias("amt"))
    tgt = DeltaTable.forName(batch_df.sparkSession, "gold.customer_spend")
    (tgt.alias("t").merge(sums.alias("s"), "t.customer_id = s.customer_id")
        .whenMatchedUpdate(condition=f"t.last_batch_id < {batch_id}",
                           set={"total": "t.total + s.amt", "last_batch_id": F.lit(batch_id)})
        .whenNotMatchedInsert(values={"customer_id": "s.customer_id", "total": "s.amt",
                                      "last_batch_id": F.lit(batch_id)})
        .execute())
payments.writeStream.foreachBatch(add_totals).option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/spend").start()
```

**Checking:** "add to total" is **not idempotent** — a retried batch would add twice. Recording `last_batch_id` per row (or using Delta's `txnAppId`/`txnVersion` options on writes) makes it safe. Alternative: use a streaming aggregation (`groupBy().sum()` in update mode) and let Spark's state handle it.

#### Q17. Write a stream to Kafka

Publish enriched orders to `orders.enriched.v1`, keyed by `order_id`.

```text
(enriched.select(F.col("order_id").cast("string").alias("key"),
                 F.to_json(F.struct("*")).alias("value"))
   .writeStream.format("kafka")
   .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", BROKERS)
   .option("topic", "orders.enriched.v1")
   .option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/orders_enriched")
   .start())
```

**Checking:** the Kafka sink needs `key`/`value` columns (string or binary); key keeps per-order ordering; Kafka sink is at-least-once — downstream consumers dedup by key/event ID.

#### Q18. Start from a point in time and limit batch size

After an incident, reprocess a topic from 2026-01-15 00:00 UTC with a new checkpoint, without overloading the cluster.

```python norun
replay = (spark.readStream.format("kafka")
          .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", BROKERS)
          .option("subscribe", "orders.v1")
          .option("startingTimestamp", "1768435200000")        # epoch millis for 2026-01-
15T00:00:00Z
          .option("maxOffsetsPerTrigger", 200_000)
          .load())
```

**Checking:** `startingTimestamp` (or `startingOffsetsByTimestamp` per partition) applies only to a new checkpoint; rate limiting keeps batches stable during catch-up; the sink must be idempotent because of the overlap with already-processed data.

#### Q19. Monitor and stop a stream safely

Print progress every minute and stop the stream gracefully when a stop-marker file appears.

```python norun
import time, json
q = df.writeStream.format("delta").option("checkpointLocation", "/chk/q").toTable("t")
while q.isActive:
    p = q.lastProgress
    if p:
        print(json.dumps({"batch": p["batchId"], "in_rps": p["inputRowsPerSecond"],
                          "proc_rps": p["processedRowsPerSecond"],
                          "ms": p["durationMs"].get("triggerExecution")}))
    if any(f.name == "stop_q" for f in dbutils.fs.ls("/ctl/")):     # marker file present
        while q.status["isTriggerActive"]:
            time.sleep(1)
        q.stop()
    time.sleep(60)
```

**Checking:** `lastProgress` metrics (input vs processing rate, duration); waiting for `isTriggerActive` to be false before `stop()`; checkpoint makes restart safe either way. (Off Databricks, check the marker with your storage SDK or `os.path.exists`.)

#### Q20. Kafka consumer in plain Python with safe commits

Without Spark: consume `orders.v1`, insert into PostgreSQL in batches, never lose data, and tolerate duplicates.

```python norun
from confluent_kafka import Consumer
import json, psycopg
c = Consumer({"bootstrap.servers": BROKERS, "group.id": "orders-to-pg",
              "enable.auto.commit": False, "auto.offset.reset": "earliest"})
c.subscribe(["orders.v1"])
with psycopg.connect(PG_DSN) as conn:
    while True:
        msgs = c.consume(num_messages=500, timeout=1.0)
        rows = [json.loads(m.value()) for m in msgs if m.error() is None]
        if not rows:
            continue
        with conn.cursor() as cur:
            cur.executemany("""INSERT INTO orders (order_id, status, amount, event_ts)
                               VALUES (%(order_id)s, %(status)s, %(amount)s, %(event_ts)s)
                               ON CONFLICT (order_id) DO UPDATE
                               SET status = EXCLUDED.status, amount = EXCLUDED.amount,
                                   event_ts = EXCLUDED.event_ts
                               WHERE orders.event_ts < EXCLUDED.event_ts""", rows)
        conn.commit()                       # 1. data committed
        c.commit(asynchronous=False)        # 2. then offsets → at-least-once, upsert makes it
idempotent
```

**Checking:** manual commit **after** the database commit (at-least-once); upsert with an event-time guard makes duplicates and out-of-order events harmless; batching for throughput. A crash between steps 1 and 2 replays the batch safely.

#### Q21. Test a streaming transformation

Write a test proving duplicates are removed and late events beyond the watermark are dropped.

    src, chk, out = str(tmp_path / "in"), str(tmp_path / "chk"), str(tmp_path / "out")
    spark.createDataFrame([("e1", "2026-01-15T10:00:00"), ("e1", "2026-01-15T10:00:00"),
                           ("e2", "2026-01-15T10:01:00")], "event_id string, event_ts string") \
         .write.json(src)

#### What isn't supported on streaming DataFrames

Knowing these saves you in live coding rounds:

| Not supported (directly) | What to do instead |
|---|---|
| `orderBy` / `sort` (except on aggregates in complete mode) | Sort inside `foreachBatch`, or in the sink/query layer |
| `limit` / `take(n)` | `foreachBatch`, or limit when reading the output |
| `countDistinct` | `approx_count_distinct`, or dedup then count |
| Window functions (`row_number`, `lag`) over a stream | `foreachBatch` (batch DataFrame), or stateful processing |
| `distinct()` without bounds | `dropDuplicates` with a watermark |
| Actions like `count()`, `collect()`, `show()` | Write to a sink; use `foreachBatch` or the memory sink for debugging |
| Outer stream–stream joins without watermarks | Add watermarks on both sides + time-range condition |
| `complete` mode without aggregation | Use append/update |

> **Memory hook:** "If it needs to see the whole table, a stream can't do it directly — do it per batch (`foreachBatch`) or per window."

title: Glossary
md:
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Unbounded data | Data that never ends — a stream |
| Event | An immutable record of something that happened, with a timestamp and key |
| Event time | When the event happened |
| Processing time | When the system processed the event |
| Window | A bucket of events by time (tumbling, sliding, session) |
| Watermark | Estimate of event-time progress; max event time minus allowed lateness |
| Late event | Event arriving after the watermark passed its time |
| State | Information remembered across events (counts, last values, buffered rows) |
| State store | Storage for state (memory, RocksDB), checkpointed for recovery |
| Checkpoint | Durable record of progress (offsets, commits, state) |
| Micro-batch | Processing a stream as a series of small batches |
| Trigger | When the next micro-batch runs |
| Output mode | What is written each batch (append, update, complete) |
| Offset | Position in a partitioned log |
| Consumer lag | How far a consumer is behind the latest data |
| At-least-once | No loss, possible duplicates |
| Exactly-once / effectively- once | Each event affects the result once |
| Idempotent | Applying the same write twice gives the same result |
| Backpressure / rate limiting | Controlling intake so processing isn't overwhelmed |
| DLQ | Dead-letter queue/topic for records that can't be processed |
| CDC | Change Data Capture — stream of inserts, updates, deletes from a database log |
| LSN / binlog position | Database log position used to order CDC events |
| Changelog | A stream of changes to a table |
| Compaction | Keeping only the latest record per key in a log |
| Savepoint | Manual snapshot of a Flink job's state for upgrades and migrations |
| Session window | Window per key that closes after a gap of inactivity |
| Stream–static join | Joining a stream with a table read each batch |
| Stream–stream join | Joining two streams with buffered state |
| Lambda / Kappa | Two-path (batch + speed) vs single-path streaming architectures |

> Streaming in one sentence: **process events by when they happened, wait a measured**

**amount for late ones, remember only what you need and forget on time, record your progress, and make every write safe to repeat.**
